title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of cross-site request forgery (csrf) in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Understanding CSRF and State-changing requests.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study cross-site request forgery (csrf) as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 95 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP security depends on server-side controls, safe data handling, and IIS/Windows configuration—not on hiding a button or filtering a string. For 'Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)', use parameterized SQL, context-aware output encoding, CSRF protections for state-changing authenticated requests, secure session handling, least privilege, and safe generic errors. Review legacy code in an authorized test copy and do not test against systems without permission.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Understanding CSRF; State-changing requests; Anti-CSRF token concepts; Validating tokens on the server; Cookie and origin considerations; Protecting administrative operations. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
content_blocks.code:
<%
If Request.ServerVariables("REQUEST_METHOD") = "POST" Then
  If CStr(Request.Form("csrfToken")) <> CStr(Session("csrfToken")) Then
    Response.Status = "403 Forbidden"
    Response.Write "Request could not be verified."
    Response.End
  End If
End If
%>
content_blocks.expected_output: A POST with a missing or mismatched session-bound token is rejected.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Generate tokens using a cryptographically secure mechanism in a reviewed component, bind them to the session, rotate them when appropriate, and never accept a token from a URL. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use an authorized local copy and benign synthetic data. Verify the expected denial/error path as well as the permitted path; never expose real secrets in examples or logs. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of cross-site request forgery (csrf). 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of cross-site request forgery (csrf) using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Understanding CSRF. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

summary: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is one step in the larger Classic ASP request, state, data, security, or maintenance workflow.

The syllabus coverage includes Understanding CSRF; State-changing requests; Anti-CSRF token concepts; Validating tokens on the server; Cookie and origin considerations; Protecting administrative operations.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.
expected_output: A POST with a missing or mismatched session-bound token is rejected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
